response.title: A Wetland Recovery Project
response.passage: Our school science club began studying a wetland near town after frogs became harder to find. The students learned that the frogs’ habitat had grown smaller as nearby building work filled shallow pools. During a dry month, water was scarce, so the club asked families to conserve water at home. At the wetland, they used simple markers to monitor the water level each week. They also marked off a section where fragile frog eggs rested among the reeds. After learning which pools dried first, the students worked with park staff to restore one damaged area. The staff showed them how to remove litter without disturbing the eggs. To decide whether the work helped, the club needed reliable records rather than guesses. They took photos from the same spots and wrote down each week’s water level. This evidence showed that the restored pool held water longer and that more frogs appeared by summer. The students shared their results at school and reminded others that small actions can protect local wildlife.

response.title: A Garden for the School Fair
response.passage: Our environmental club started a small herb garden behind the school in early spring. The goal was to create a display for families visiting the school fair. At eight on Saturday, our class would go to the community garden together, since the bus was booked and a gardening session was ready for us. Before touching the soil, each student had to take a pair of gloves from the supply table and put them on. Mia offered to look after the seedlings for the weekend. She planned to water them each morning and check that their pots stayed damp, rather than search for them or simply glance at them once. The rest of the club would return on Monday to finish the display. That day, our team would carry out a short survey by asking visitors to identify herbs by smell. We would record their answers first and compare them later, so this was the data-gathering step. Several classmates were interested in the project; they signed up for extra shifts and asked to plant more herbs because they wanted to learn about them. On fair day, families could touch the leaves and compare their scents. By the end, the club had a garden display and a clear record of what visitors had learned.

response.title: A Garden Shared by Two Clubs
response.passage:
The science club planned a small vegetable garden beside the library. Since each member brought a different skill, the students agreed to cooperate rather than leave all the work to one person. Mina measured the space, while Leo checked which vegetables could grow in shade. After comparing Mina’s measurements with Leo’s list of shade-tolerant vegetables, the club chose to reserve one corner for herbs the cooking club might need later. To place the remaining boxes well, the students decided to observe how sunlight reached the area at different times of day. Their observations showed that the wall blocked afternoon sun, so they moved the boxes to a brighter spot.

In early May, a shortage of clean pots threatened the planting schedule. The club counted its supplies and found only six usable pots, although ten seedlings were ready. The students asked the art class for help, and together they cleaned old paint containers for reuse. The recycled containers gave each seedling a safe place to grow without delaying the project. By the end of the month, the garden was growing well, and both clubs were proud of their shared work.

response.extraOption: The storage room contained ten clean pots, more than enough for all the seedlings.

response.title: A Safe Visit to Pine Creek
response.passage:
The environmental club planned to measure water clarity at Pine Creek. After rain flooded the path beside the creek, Ms. Wu moved the group’s meeting point to a raised platform. Before they left school, she checked the park office’s daily report. The report was reliable because park staff posted water levels before opening each morning. It warned that the current under the footbridge was unusually strong after the storm. The students packed clear jars and a measuring chart, but left their wading boots at school.

At the platform, a guide asked them to compare the creek with a photograph taken before the rain. Unlike the old picture, today’s surface carried small branches quickly toward the bend. This movement made the danger easy to notice, although the water near the bank looked shallow. They recorded the water’s color from above instead of entering the creek. Back at school, they used their notes to explain why testing water should never come before safety.
removals: After rain flooded the path beside the creek, Ms. Wu moved the group’s meeting point to a raised platform.

response.title: Reporting on the Bus Route
response.passage:
The newspaper editor gave Nia two bus maps to compare for a report on service changes. She began with the current map, which the transit office had updated that week. Its blue marks showed two new stops near the hospital. A notice beside the route map gave the reason for the added stops. It explained that construction had closed the old road, so buses now used the avenue beside the hospital. Nia wanted readers to know whether this change would last after construction ended.

A librarian found a city plan from last spring for Nia to check. The plan showed the old road reopening in October. Nia then called the transit office to ask whether buses would return to their former route in October. The reply said that no final decision had been made. Nia described the route as it operated that week and advised riders to check again later.

response.title: A Smarter Way to Water the Garden
response.passage:
When the school garden club prepared its spring planting day, it expected twenty volunteers. The city had advised residents to limit outdoor water use after weeks without rain. To divide the work, the students agreed to cooperate instead of letting each team water at random. One group measured the soil, while another checked how much water each bed needed.

At first, the club believed the two rain barrels would be enough. By Friday, however, the barrels held only a quarter of the water the planting plan required, so the club faced a serious shortage. The students then asked the cafeteria to save clean rinse water from washing vegetables. They placed a marked bucket beside the sink and explained that only vegetable-rinse water should go into it. During lunch, one student agreed to observe the bucket and record the amount every fifteen minutes.

The first day's notes showed that the bucket filled twice as fast as expected. That extra supply allowed the club to water the seedlings without opening the outdoor tap. Even so, they chose to reserve one full bucket for emergencies instead of using every drop that afternoon. When the next dry week arrived, the saved water kept the youngest plants alive, and the club shared its collection method with another school.
removals: To divide the work, the students agreed to cooperate instead of letting each team water at random.

response.title: Finding a Safe Place by the Creek
response.passage:
The environmental club planned to measure water movement in a creek before choosing a site for a cleanup. After a night of rain, the creek looked calm from the bank, but its surface told only part of the story. Ms. Chen brought a reliable flow meter, whose measurements had matched a professional team's during last year's survey. Its digital display showed how quickly the water moved past a point.

At the first bend, two readings differed sharply, even though the students had held the meter at the same depth. The group did not accept either number as correct without checking the equipment. They repeated the test with a second meter and found that its sensor was loose. Once they had a dependable reading, Ms. Chen showed them how to compare speeds at different points. The current was strongest near the narrow center of the creek and slower beside the bank.

That steady movement carried floating leaves toward a quiet pocket below the footbridge. Since the club wanted volunteers to work safely, the students chose that sheltered bank as their meeting point. They marked the spot with orange tape and sent its location to the school office. On cleanup day, everyone gathered there, and the earlier measurements helped them keep the group away from the faster water.
removals: Ms. Chen brought a reliable flow meter, whose measurements had matched a professional team's during last year's survey.

response.extraOption: The club poured cooking oil into the creek so the students could see which way the water moved.

response.title: Keeping the Bus Map Up to Date
response.passage:
When the town library planned a display about neighborhood history, volunteers began with old photographs and maps. They soon faced a problem: some details had changed so recently that the old records could mislead visitors. For instance, the team wanted to include the bus network because many residents relied on it to reach the library. The map in the archive showed a route that had been moved two years earlier.

The display therefore needed current information, not simply the newest-looking document in the collection. A student volunteer contacted the transit office and asked for its latest route list. The office sent a digital file, but it included a temporary detour that would end the following week. To avoid presenting that short-term change as permanent, the team checked the date and notes attached to each route. They then compared the file with notices posted at the bus stops near the library.

This second check revealed that one stop had closed for construction, although the closure was missing from the file. The students added a clear note explaining both the regular route and the temporary closure. They also printed the date on which the information had been checked, so visitors could judge how recently it had been updated. At the opening, a visitor used the display to choose a bus, and later emailed the library to report a newly moved stop.
removals: They soon faced a problem: some details had changed so recently that the old records could mislead visitors.
The display therefore needed current information, not simply the newest-looking document in the collection.

response.title: A Garden Through the Dry Weeks
response.passage: At the start of May, the science club planned a small garden behind the school. Because the water tank was old, the members worried there might be a shortage during the dry weeks. They agreed to cooperate: two students checked the soil each morning, while others collected rainwater. The caretaker was reliable; whenever the club needed tools, he arrived with the shed key. Before planting, Mei asked the club to reserve half the collected water for seedlings that had not sprouted. For three days, Ben observed the garden at lunch and wrote down which beds dried fastest. His notes showed that the sunny bed lost water sooner, so the club moved its new pots beside the wall. When a brief shower came, they filled the tank but kept the saved half for the seedlings as planned. By June, the seedlings were healthy, and the club chose the same plan for its next garden.

response.title: Following the River’s Flow
response.passage: The environmental club visited a local river for a science project. Since the banks were slippery, their teacher marked a viewing area on the dry path and told them not to enter the water. At an upstream marker, the students placed three small sticks in the river, one after another. A steady current carried each stick downstream past a lower marker in seconds. To check the direction, they released corks from the same spot and watched from the bank. All the corks moved toward a bend, and none traveled back toward the starting point. The students noted the markers’ positions and drew arrows on a map to show the water’s movement. Before leaving, they compared their maps, which all showed the flow heading toward the bend.

response.title: A Careful Plan for the Garden
response.passage: After two weeks without rain, the school garden faced a shortage of water. The science club had planted young bean plants, and several leaves were beginning to curl. Rather than water every bed equally, club members agreed to cooperate on a plan. They would use the small tank beside the greenhouse only for the youngest plants. They would reserve the water collected in two covered barrels for days when the tap was turned off. Each morning, one student would observe the soil near the roots and record whether it felt dry. Ms. Chen, who checked the records, said the notes were reliable because different students made the same observations on several mornings. On Friday, the students found that the older plants still had firm leaves, while the youngest ones were dry. They used water from the tank on the young plants and left the barrel water untouched. By the next week, the younger plants had recovered, and the club kept its daily checks in place.

response.title: Following the Stream
response.passage: On Thursday, Ms. Wu’s class visited a narrow stream behind their school. Their assignment was to compare the water’s clarity at two marked spots, not to collect animals. Ms. Wu asked each team to release a small leaf at a starting line and time how long it took to reach a stick downstream. The leaf moved steadily toward the stick, carried by the current. At the straight upper stretch, it took eight seconds to travel the marked distance. At a shaded bend, the same distance took nineteen seconds. One student guessed that the bend’s water was moving faster because it looked darker. However, the teams repeated the test three times, and the leaf was slower at the bend each time. Ms. Wu asked them to report the timed results separately from their visual impressions. In their final notes, the students concluded that the current carried the leaf faster at the straight stretch than at the bend.

response.title: A Campaign Still in Progress
response.passage: At the start of April, the student council launched a four-week campaign to reduce disposable cups. Its current goal is to encourage students to bring reusable bottles, not to ban the cafeteria’s paper cups. A poster left from last year still says that all drinks will be served in personal cups. Because the old poster is beside the entrance, several students ask whether the rule has already changed. Council members replace it with a notice that gives the campaign dates and explains that paper cups remain available. During lunch, they count how many students use reusable bottles and record the number each day. The count rises from 38 on Monday to 61 on Friday. However, a rainy-day announcement moves Friday’s lunch period indoors, so the council decides not to compare that day’s count with the earlier ones. Instead, they plan another count next week under the usual lunch arrangement. The council will use several comparable counts to decide whether the campaign is changing habits before considering a stricter proposal.
